facets.title: The one rule: voice is human-load-bearing; AI is everything else

facts.text: A writer's distinctive voice is the residue of their judgment. An LLM, trained on the global mean of internet prose, regresses toward that mean. The collaboration mode this skill defends keeps the human responsible for voice and uses AI for tasks where the mean is fine (mechanics, structure, length compression, format conversion).
LLMs default to five patterns:
Hedging. "It's worth noting that…"
Triadic rhythm. Three-item lists replace one strong word.
Topic-sentence tax. Every paragraph opens with a meta-sentence.
Latinate verbs. "Utilize," "facilitate," "leverage."
Bridge phrases. "Furthermore," "moreover."
delve, leverage, robust, paradigm, seamless, utilize, commence, facilitate, furthermore, navigate, landscape, cutting-edge, holistic, ecosystem, harness (verb), foster (verb)
Editing an AI-drafted email, memo, or article where the argument and facts are sound but the prose has slipped into the LLM's default mean-of-internet voice.

facts.text: Reviewing a piece of writing for the five characteristic LLM patterns — hedging, triadic rhythm, topic-sentence tax, Latinate verbs, and bridge phrases — before it goes out under a human byline.

facts.text: Treat voice as the one thing that must stay human-load-bearing in any AI-assisted writing workflow, and delegate everything else (formatting, structural scaffolding, first-draft mechanics) to the model.

facts.text: Read a draft out loud or scan it specifically for the five voice-transfer failure patterns — hedging phrases, three-item lists standing in for one strong word, meta-sentence paragraph openers, Latinate verbs, and bridge-phrase transitions.

facts.text: Run a Tier 1 banned-word pass (delve, leverage, robust, paradigm, seamless, utilize, commence, facilitate, furthermore, navigate, landscape, cutting-edge, holistic, ecosystem, harness, foster) before calling any AI-assisted draft final.

facts.text: Use the AI for mechanics-level tasks where the global mean of internet prose is genuinely fine — reformatting, summarizing, drafting boilerplate — and reserve final judgment calls about tone and framing for the human writer.

facts.text: Assuming a single banned-word scan catches every AI-ism — bridge phrases and topic-sentence tax often survive a word-level edit because they're structural, not lexical.

facts.text: A banned-word list drifts: as writers and readers adapt, yesterday's AI-tell words become normal usage or new tells emerge, so the Tier 1 list needs periodic revisiting rather than treating it as fixed.

facts.text: Scanning for these patterns is necessary but not sufficient — a draft can pass every check on this list and still carry no distinctive human judgment if the writer didn't actually make any calls before publishing.
